answer.sourceLine: This is the closing declaration in the English text of Fidel Castro’s History Will Absolve Me, his defense following the failed Moncada assault in 1953. The online translation separates the words into three sentences.

source.excerpt: Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.
trail: The translated speech ↗ ends with these three sentences.
The publication history ↗ describes the defense and the subsequent pamphlet; a later published text is not an audio record of every word spoken in court.

The archive’s source header ↗ credits translators Pedro Álvarez Tabío and Andrew Paul Booth, lists Editorial de Ciencias Sociales, Havana, 1975, and notes a recheck against the Spanish text in 1981. The 1953 date belongs to the underlying defense, not the publication date of this English translation.
source.rightsNote: The checked English text credits Pedro Álvarez Tabío and Andrew Paul Booth as translators. Its header lists Editorial de Ciencias Sociales, Havana, 1975, and says the translation was rechecked against the Spanish text in 1981. This modern English translation is treated as copyrighted; the 1953 speech date does not make its English wording public domain.

author.name: Fidel Castro
author.heading: About Fidel Castro
author.bio: Fidel Castro led the revolutionary movement that overthrew Fulgencio Batista’s government in 1959. He then governed Cuba as prime minister and president, overseeing the consolidation of a one-party communist state and a long confrontation with the United States.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Castro used his defense to turn an accusation of armed rebellion into an indictment of Batista’s government and a program for Cuba. The final appeal asks history to judge him differently from the court; it later supplied the title by which the published defense became known.
